name: Influenza
agent: Influenza viruses; URTI is a broader syndrome and is not equivalent to laboratory-confirmed influenza.
symptoms: Fever, cough, sore throat, muscle aches and fatigue.
infectious: Often from one day before symptoms until about 5–7 days afterwards; longer in some children or immunocompromised people.

name: Measles
symptoms: Fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis and a spreading rash.
incubation: First symptoms commonly begin 11–12 days after exposure; rash often follows around day 14.
infectious: Typically four days before through four days after rash onset.

name: Pertussis
symptoms: An initially mild cough may progress to repeated coughing fits; infants can have pauses in breathing.
incubation: Usually 5–10 days; symptoms can take up to three weeks.
infectious: Most infectious early in illness. Duration depends on treatment and disease stage; consult the linked guidance.

name: HFMD
agent: Enteroviruses cause hand, foot and mouth disease.
symptoms: Fever, painful mouth sores and rash on hands and feet.
incubation: Fever and early symptoms often appear 3–5 days after infection.
infectious: Usually greatest during the first week; spread can continue after symptoms resolve.
transmission: Secretions, blister fluid, contaminated surfaces and faecal contact.

name: Chickenpox
symptoms: An itchy blistering rash, fever and malaise.
infectious: From 1–2 days before rash until lesions crust; breakthrough infections without crusting need separate criteria.
transmission: Airborne spread and contact with infectious lesions.

name: Mumps
symptoms: Fever and painful swelling of the salivary glands; some infections have few symptoms.
infectious: Usually two days before through five days after salivary-gland swelling begins.
transmission: Saliva and respiratory secretions during close contact.

name: Dengue
symptoms: Fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, body aches, nausea and sometimes rash.
incubation: Symptoms usually begin 4–10 days after infection.
infectious: Transmission usually involves mosquitoes rather than routine direct contact. Timing of human-to-mosquito transmission differs from symptom duration; see WHO guidance.

name: Salmonellosis
agent: Salmonella bacteria; acute diarrhoea is a broader syndrome with many possible causes.
incubation: Commonly six hours to six days for Salmonella infection; other causes of diarrhoea differ.
infectious: Shedding may continue after symptoms improve; no single infectious period applies to all diarrhoeal illnesses.
transmission: Contaminated food, water or faecal contact.
